question: How do life insurers' promises turn into private credit and offshore reinsurance?
answer: Policy and annuity money becomes long-dated liabilities that insurers invest: long promises supply investable general-account liabilities, and insurer asset allocation directs trillions into bonds, mortgages, structured assets and alternatives, including through a private credit and structured-asset channel. The issuing life insurer can then cede liabilities and economics to an asset-intensive reinsurer, secured by a trust, funds withheld or collateral. The NAIC's September 2026 analysis estimated $1.210 trillion of private-credit exposure at year-end 2025 after removing identifiable overlaps. The annual report says total ceded premium increased 32.8% to $580.5 billion and assumed premium increased 48.1% to $272.5 billion. Treasury convened state regulators in 2026 specifically around private credit, offshore reserve movement, RBC, private letter ratings and evolving business models. The hub's limit: Offshore location, reciprocal-jurisdiction status or large ceded reserve does not alone prove weakened security or insolvency.

items.text: FIO reported that 66.8 percent of life-sector cash and invested assets were long-term bonds at year-end 2025, with mortgage loans another 13.9 percent. Privately placed bonds—including FIO's broad private-credit category—had reached 48.4 percent of life-sector bond holdings.

items.title: Private placements and the counterweight
items.sub: Big Insurance: Monetary and Government Control Map
items.text: FIO's year-end 2025 record found private placements approaching 3.6 times life-sector capital and surplus, while alternative assets reached $475.6 billion. It also preserved the counterweight: 95.4 percent of life bonds were investment grade, operating cash flow was positive and aggregate cash and invested assets exceeded general-account liabilities on a carrying-value basis.

items.title: Federal Reserve insurance-group supervision
items.sub: Monetary conditions · Applies only to covered holding companies and designated nonbanks
kv: Supervises covered depository-institution holding companies significantly engaged in insurance and applies the Building Block Approach where required.
Regulation Q aggregates capital frameworks while preserving underlying state insurance and federal bank building blocks.
The Federal Reserve does not supervise every insurer or replace state legal-entity solvency authority.

items.title: Federal Reserve policy and the yield curve
items.sub: Monetary conditions · Reprices long assets, liabilities, guarantees and borrower credit
kv: Changes risk-free rates and financial conditions that feed insurer reinvestment, valuation, hedging, product pricing and surrender behavior.
The Federal Reserve sets monetary policy; insurers make portfolio and liability decisions within markets and regulatory rules.
A policy-rate move does not order an insurer transaction or determine every long-term yield and credit spread.

research.title: How insurers invest trillions, move risk and share losses with government
research.answer: U.S. insurance runs through many separate regulators, very large insurer balance sheets, reinsurance and public loss programs that together work as one system. Each authority, company, contract and payment still keeps its own legal identity and timing.

research.title: Not a new currency: a fight over the points where money changes form
research.answer: As of July 2026, the money system looked less like one coin replacing another and more like a linked, programmable set of national systems. Power sits with whoever controls the points where deposits become collateral, collateral becomes cash, and losses get…
